evidence.claim: The 52-mile Steens Mountain Backcountry Byway traverses the mountain’s west slope and reaches 9,700 feet, the highest road elevation in Oregon.
evidence.quote: The west slope of Steens Mountain is traversed by a 52-mile (84 km) loop road, which is suitable for passenger vehicles. The road reaches an elevation of 9,700 feet (2,960 m), making it the highest road in Oregon.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents the byway as access to glacier-carved gorges, wild horse country and the Riddle Brothers Ranch National Historic District.
evidence.quote: The CMPA encompasses deep glacier-carved gorges

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents the byway as access to glacier-carved gorges, wild horse country and the Riddle Brothers Ranch National Historic District.
evidence.quote: The 52-mile Steens Mountain Backcountry Byway provides access to four campgrounds, numerous trails, the Riddle Brothers Ranch National Historic District, wild horse roaming areas, and opportunities for fishing and hunting.

evidence.claim: The mountain’s east face is built from stacked basalt flows that inundated the region between 17 and 14 million years ago.
evidence.quote: The east face of Steens Mountain is composed mainly of basalts stacked one upon another. Lava flows several hundreds of feet thick inundated the region between 17 and 14 million years ago.

evidence.claim: Its western face slopes more gradually than its almost vertical eastern face, with canyons cut through basalt reaching depths of half a mile.
evidence.quote: Although its eastern face is almost vertical, its western face slopes more gradually. Cut through basalt, the western canyons are up to 1⁄2 mile (0.80 km) deep.

evidence.claim: In 2000, a law approved by President Bill Clinton created the Steens Mountain Cooperative Management and Protection Area.
evidence.quote: On October 24, 2000, President Bill Clinton approved the Steens Mountain Cooperative Management and Protective Act.

evidence.claim: In 2000, a law approved by President Bill Clinton created the Steens Mountain Cooperative Management and Protection Area.
evidence.quote: This act created the Steens Mountain BLM Cooperative Management and Protection Area

evidence.claim: Local landowners and government representatives developed the act in response to a proposed national monument.
evidence.quote: The act was created by local landowners in cooperation with local and national government representatives in response to a proposed National Monument.

evidence.claim: The resulting landscape includes public and private land as well as specially designated areas with particular regulations.
evidence.quote: The Steens Mountain CMPA is a mixture of public and private lands and specially designated areas where particular regulations may apply.

evidence.claim: The loop road leaves Highway 205 just past Frenchglen.
evidence.quote: Just past Frenchglen, turn left onto the Steens Mountain Loop Road.

evidence.quote: Whorehouse Meadow is a meadow located on the western slope of Steens Mountain southeast of Frenchglen

evidence.claim: Whorehouse Meadow lies on Steens Mountain’s western slope, southeast of Frenchglen.
evidence.quote: Whorehouse Meadow is a meadow located on the western slope of Steens Mountain southeast of Frenchglen, Oregon, United States.

evidence.claim: Bureau of Land Management maps substituted Naughty Girl Meadow in the 1960s, but public outcry led to restoration of the older name in 1981.
evidence.quote: The name was changed in the 1960s to "Naughty Girl Meadow" on Bureau of Land Management maps, but in 1981 the old name was restored after public outcry.

evidence.claim: Women from Vale had set up wood-and-canvas tents here to serve local sheepherders and cattlemen.
evidence.quote: Entrepreneuring women from Vale, Oregon, would set up wood and canvas tents in the meadow to provide services to the sheepherders and cattlemen of the area.

evidence.claim: Many herders were Basque American immigrants. Their carvings, sometimes explicit, remain in the surrounding aspens.
evidence.quote: Many of the sheepherders were Basque American immigrants, and their sometimes explicit carvings can still be found in the bark of aspen trees surrounding the meadow.

evidence.claim: The meadow now lies within the Steens Mountain Wilderness.
evidence.quote: It lies within the Steens Mountain Wilderness.

evidence.claim: Lewis McArthur’s Oregon Geographic Names locates it a mile east of Fish Lake and describes it as accessible but secluded.
evidence.quote: Lewis McArthur, writing about the landmark in Oregon Geographic Names, describes it as an "accessible but secluded meadow a mile east of Fish Lake."

evidence.claim: Little Blitzen Gorge carries a river through a U-shaped trench cut by ice into the western face of Steens Mountain.
evidence.quote: Little Blitzen Gorge, down which the river flows, is one of four huge U-shaped trenches carved by ice on the western face of Steens Mountain during the most recent glacial period.

evidence.claim: BLM includes its overlook among the byway’s viewpoints.
evidence.quote: The views from Kiger Gorge, East Rim, Big Indian Gorge, Wildhorse, and Little Blitzen Gorge overlooks

evidence.claim: The Little Blitzen runs 12.5 miles, and Congress designated that whole stretch Wild and Scenic in 1988.
evidence.quote: As part of the Omnibus Oregon Wild and Scenic Rivers Act of 1988, Congress designated "the 12.5-mile segment of the Little Blitzen from its headwaters to its confluence with the South Fork Blitzen" as Wild and Scenic.

evidence.claim: In 2000 it became part of the nation’s first Great Basin redband trout reserve.
evidence.quote: It is part of the nation's first Great Basin redband trout reserve, established by Congress in 2000.
